title: Ghadir Khumm
hookLine: both traditions report the Prophet ﷺ saying, of whomever I am his mawla, Ali is his mawla, and they read it differently

cards: A watering place on the road between Mecca and Medina, called Khumm. Tradition knows the spot as Ghadir Khumm, the pool of Khumm.
The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, stops there with the people traveling with him, and stands up to speak. Sahih Muslim records the scene through the companion Zayd ibn Arqam.
The Prophet says he is only a human being, and that the messenger of his Lord will soon come for him. He is speaking like someone saying goodbye. Today: Ghadir Khumm.

teach.b: In Muslim's report, the Prophet goes on: I am leaving among you two weighty things. The first is the Book of God, in which is guidance and light, so hold fast to it. The second is the people of my house.
And he says, more than once: I remind you of God concerning the people of my house. Then the line at the center of today.

teach.h: OF WHOMEVER I AM HIS MAWLA.
teach.b: Al-Tirmidhi records it: of whomever I am his mawla, Ali is his mawla. Sunni and Shia collections both carry these words, and both communities honor them. They read them differently because of one word.
Mawla carries more than one meaning. A few days ago it described Salim, the freed man linked to Abu Hudhayfah's house.
Readers of this hadith have heard in it friend, ally, protector, patron, or master. In the Sunni reading, it means love and loyalty here: whoever takes me as his friend should love and stand by Ali.
Some of them connect it to a tension reported in Bukhari: Buraydah, who had been with Ali on a mission, resented him, and the Prophet told him not to hate Ali.
In this reading, Ghadir is a public defense of Ali and a call to love him.
Shia Muslims read mawla here as master, the one with authority over the believers.

In their reading, the Prophet is naming his successor in front of the people, by God's command, and the words about his household point the same way. Shia communities mark the day as a festival, Eid al-Ghadir.
Same pool, same sentence: two readings, held with deep conviction, each with its scholars and its reasons.

how: Sunni and Shia Muslims both narrate the hadith of Ghadir Khumm; Shia Muslims celebrate Eid al-Ghadir as the day the Prophet designated Ali, while Sunni scholars teach it as a call to love and support Ali.

games.q: you hear the words: of whomever I am his mawla, Ali is his mawla. what does mawla mean here?
o: friend and ally, to be loved and supported.
master and leader, appointed to guide.
both readings have their scholars and their reasons.
games.why: Sunni scholars read friend and ally; Shia Muslims read master and leader. the same words, two readings.

practice: Say the line to yourself slowly: of whomever I am his mawla, Ali is his mawla. On one breath, hear it the first way: friend, ally, someone to love and stand beside.
On the next, hear it the second way: master, leader, the one appointed to guide. Don't choose; just notice how much one word can carry.

wordCard.voice: Ghadir Khumm. The pool of Khumm, between Mecca and Medina, where the Prophet spoke of the Book and his household, and said of Ali: of whomever I am his mawla, Ali is his mawla. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: a word with a wide range: friend, ally, protector, patron, master.

carryVoice: Your line: the same words, two readings. One sentence, honored by both. See you tomorrow.
